title: Phase 1: Requirements, domain model and architecture
description: Define the core requirements, bounded contexts, and layered architecture for the Enterprise Expense Platform. Model the domain with aggregate roots, value objects, and explicit transaction boundaries before writing a single line of infrastructure code.

data.text: Every senior engineer knows that the cost of architectural mistakes grows exponentially over time. In this phase, you'll resist the temptation to scaffold controllers and jump straight into database tables. Instead, you'll spend quality time understanding the business domain, identifying aggregate boundaries, and locking in the event flow that will drive your system for years.
The platform must support the following core capabilities. Each maps to an explicit set of user stories and acceptance criteria that you'll validate in later phases.

data.title: Core capabilities
items: Employees submit expense reports containing multiple line items (meals, travel, lodging, software).
Each line item may have an attached receipt image stored as a blob.
A configurable expense policy engine validates submissions against per-category limits, per-project caps, and mandatory receipt rules.
Multi-level approval: direct manager → department head → finance (configurable per organization).
Approvers see only reports within their cost center or delegated authority scope.
Finance can reimburse approved reports and export them to accounting software.
Employees view their submission history; managers see their team's pending approvals.
Admins manage organizations, departments, users, and policy rules.

data.text: A clear aggregate boundary prevents distributed transactions, race conditions, and overly broad repository methods. In the expense domain, **ExpenseReport** is the natural aggregate root. Everything that must be saved atomically lives inside it.

terms.definition: An entity that controls access to its internal objects. All external references go through the root (e.g., ExpenseReport), never directly to child entities (LineItem, Approval).
An immutable object defined by its attributes rather than identity (e.g., Money, EmailAddress, PolicyRule).
A semantic boundary within which a particular domain model is defined and applicable. ExpenseSubmission and PolicyEngine are separate bounded contexts.
A record of something significant that happened in the domain (e.g., ExpenseReportSubmitted, ApprovalGranted), published for other contexts to react.

data.title: Why ExpenseReport is the aggregate root
data.text: If two users concurrently modify LineItems on the same report, you need one transaction, one lock, one validation pass. That coherence boundary is exactly what an aggregate root enforces. Never inject an ILineItemRepository directly — it breaks the aggregate invariant.

data.title: Supporting aggregates
items: PolicyRule: per-organization expense policy (category limit, project cap, receipt requirement). Owned by Admin.
Organization: tenant boundary; all queries filter by OrganizationId.
Department: organizational unit within an Organization; links to a CostCenter.
CostCenter: budget owner; tied to a GL code for accounting export.
UserProfile: employee record with department, managerId, and role assignments.

data.text: We use a strict layered architecture enforced by project boundaries. Inner layers never reference outer layers.

data.title: Project layers
items: **Expense.Domain**: Entities, value objects, domain events, repository interfaces, business rules. No infrastructure references.
**Expense.Application**: CQRS handlers (MediatR), validators (FluentValidation), DTOs, application service interfaces.
**Expense.Infrastructure**: EF Core DbContext, repository implementations, external service clients, outbox publisher.
**Expense.Api**: ASP.NET Core controllers, middleware, auth, health checks, OpenAPI configuration.
**Expense.Web**: React 19 + Vite app (separate repo or sibling folder).

data.title: Avoid the common layering mistake
data.text: It's tempting to let controllers query DbContext directly. Resist. Handlers in Expense.Application own the use-case orchestration. Controllers should be thin (max 15 lines). This separation enables unit-testing handlers without WebApplicationFactory.

data.title: C# domain model: ExpenseReport as aggregate root
data.content: The aggregate root exposes behavior, not setters. External code cannot arbitrarily change Status or TotalAmount.

data.title: C# value object: Money
data.content: Value objects enforce invariants at construction time and make currency explicit across the domain.

data.text: When an ExpenseReport is approved, several things must happen: the approver's task list must clear, the employee must be notified, and the accounting export job must be scheduled. These side effects do not belong inside the aggregate — they are the responsibility of event handlers in the Application or Infrastructure layer.

data.title: Key domain events
items: ExpenseReportSubmitted → trigger policy validation, create approval chain, notify first approver.
ApprovalGranted → advance chain or mark approved; if all approved, notify employee and finance.
ExpenseReportRejected → notify submitter with reason; reopen draft status.
ExpenseReportPaid → trigger accounting export, mark as reimbursed.

data.title: Event naming convention
data.text: Use past-tense names (ExpenseReportSubmitted, not SubmitExpenseReport). This removes ambiguity: the event signals that something already happened, not a command to do something.

items.question: Why not use EF Core entities directly as domain models?
items.answer: EF Core entities couple persistence concerns (navigation properties, lazy loading, annotations) to domain logic. Separating them lets you evolve the schema without breaking domain rules and keeps unit tests fast and dependency-free.

items.question: Should Approval be its own aggregate?
items.answer: No. An Approval is a part of the ExpenseReport aggregate — it cannot exist without the report, and all approvals for a report must be loaded and validated together. If you need to query "all approvals pending for a user," that is a read-model concern (Phase 2+), not a separate aggregate.

data.title: Phase 1 summary
points: ExpenseReport is the aggregate root; line items, approvals, and receipts are children.
Supporting aggregates (Organization, Department, PolicyRule) enforce tenant and policy boundaries.
Layered architecture: Domain → Application → Infrastructure → Api.
Domain events drive side effects without polluting aggregate logic.
Spend extra time here — bad domain boundaries are the hardest thing to refactor later.
data.takeaway: Domain modeling is not a one-time activity. Revisit the model when requirements shift, but the aggregate boundaries you set in Phase 1 will define your system's integrity guarantees.
